baseline.happiness_note: the simulation's match with real happiness surveys in its own 2015-2023 run
baseline.migration: see the live figure on the home page

fixes.text: Who actually leaves a country now follows money sent home from abroad and the share of immigrants living there, as well as how many simulated people want to leave. The world's yearly total of migrants still matches the real figure; only which countries they come from shifts. Each variable's push is capped so it can't swamp the simulation.

Refugee flows from war zones had no upper limit, so over 31 simulated years some countries emptied (Yemen fell below a million people) and their neighbours overfilled. Flight is now capped at 12% of a country a year, about the worst ever recorded, and every country was put back to its real share of the world's population.
Crackdowns follow real records: police break up some protests even in democracies, and deadly force is now rarer and separate (Mass Mobilization data).

items.name: Minimum wage, for the country's wealth
items.what: How far the lowest legal pay goes, in purchasing-power dollars, compared with what the country's income per person would predict.

quick.note: against the model's inputs, not the simulation

items.why: Inside the simulation it barely moved happiness on unseen countries and made migration slightly worse. The simulation already captures most of what it adds.

items.name: Healthy life expectancy
items.what: Years a newborn can expect to live in good health.
items.source: WHO, via Our World in Data
items.why: Passed the happiness test: on unseen countries it lifted the match from 0.82 to 0.84 and from 0.74 to 0.78, at the strongest setting tried. A second round tries stronger settings, and tries it combined with food insecurity, since the two partly measure the same hardship. No help for migration (−0.01 and +0.07).

items.name: Food insecurity
items.what: Share of people who skipped meals or ran out of food in the past year.
items.source: UN FAO, via the World Bank
items.why: Passed the happiness test by about as much as life expectancy (0.82 to 0.84, 0.74 to 0.78 on unseen countries). Caution: it comes from the same Gallup poll as the happiness surveys, so part of the gain may be that overlap. The second round tests it combined with life expectancy, which has no such overlap.

items.name: Social safety net
items.what: Share of people covered by at least one social protection or labour programme.
items.why: Strong in the quick check, but inside the simulation it barely moved happiness on unseen countries (+0.004 and +0.005). Only 96 mostly lower-income countries have figures, which leaves most of the world unchanged.

items.name: Years of schooling
items.what: Average years of education of people aged 15 to 64.
items.source: Our World in Data (Lee-Lee and Barro-Lee)
items.why: Small and uneven inside the simulation: +0.004 on one half of the countries, +0.018 on the other. The simulation already gets most of this from income.

items.name: Money sent home from abroad
items.what: Remittances received, as a share of the economy.
items.why: Passed: on unseen countries it lifted the migration ranking from about 0.03 to 0.31 and 0.36; together with immigrants, to 0.30 and 0.55. Chain migration is real (people follow family who already left), though remittances partly measure that past emigration itself.

live.note: Live migration score before: 0.12 (rank match, 121 countries). After: measured once the first full simulated year on the new engine closes.

items.name: Immigrants already living there
items.what: Share of residents born in another country.
items.source: UN DESA, via the World Bank
items.why: Passed, with a question mark: 0.19 and 0.43 on unseen countries. Small, open countries with many immigrants also lose many people, so it may be measuring how mobile a country is rather than what draws people in.

live.note: Live migration score before: 0.12 (rank match, 121 countries). After: measured once the first full simulated year on the new engine closes.

items.name: Corruption
items.what: How corrupt the public sector is seen to be by experts and businesses.
items.source: Transparency International, via Our World in Data
items.why: Rejected for migration: on unseen countries it made the ranking worse (−0.20 and −0.12), and the best strength flipped sign between halves.

items.name: Visa freedom, for the country's geography
items.what: Countries its passport can enter without a visa, weighted by land neighbours and the country's size.
items.source: Passport Index dataset (open data) and the World Bank
items.why: Rejected: worse on unseen countries in both halves (−0.11 and −0.12).

items.name: Civil liberties
items.what: How free people are to speak, gather and move.
items.source: V-Dem v16, via Our World in Data (political civil liberties index, built from indicators of government repression)
items.why: Small gain for happiness (+0.02), none for migration. Checked again against the real-world copy of the simulation: in the 30 most repressed countries the surveys come out 0.09 points below the simulation, and in the 30 freest, 0.33 above. So there's no sign that people in repressive countries overstate their happiness in surveys; if anything, the simulation rates repressive countries slightly too happy next to free ones. Controlling for income the effect is small and not certain (−0.28 ± 0.20 points).

items.name: Air pollution
items.why: Its migration gain comes from Gulf states, which are polluted and also take in many migrants. Pollution isn't what draws people.

items.name: Disasters
items.what: People newly displaced by floods, storms, droughts and earthquakes, per person.

items.name: Living alone (a stand-in for sociability)
items.what: Share of households with one person, latest year 2000-2018 (most around 2013).
items.source: UN household size data, via Our World in Data
items.why: Not a clean measure of sociability. Once the simulation is accounted for, countries where more people live alone are happier, not lonelier: it tracks wealth and independence (Sweden 43%, Germany 42%, Pakistan 1%). Its migration gain comes from the same wealth link, since rich countries draw migrants.

items.name: Sociability, as a personal trait
items.what: Each simulated person gets their own sociability: how many people they meet and how much connection they need to feel all right, so a loner and a social person react differently to living alone or in a crowded city.
items.source: To be tuned against county loneliness data in the California calibration
items.why: There's no clean country-by-country measure (the obvious survey questions come from the same poll as the happiness surveys, and living alone tracks wealth instead), so this would be tested on people, not countries: does it help the California model match real loneliness by county?

items.name: How governments answer protests
items.what: How often police break up or arrest protesters, and how often they use deadly force, by kind of government.
items.source: Mass Mobilization Protest Data v5.1 (Clark & Regan, 15,239 protests against governments in 162 countries, 1990-2020, CC0); V-Dem v16 via Our World in Data

quick.note: 138 countries with 15+ protests; rules tuned on half the countries, scored on the other half

items.why: Before: democracies never broke up a protest, and autocracies did so 55% of the time, always as a heavy crackdown. Real records show police break up or arrest protesters in about a quarter of protests even in democracies, and deadly force is rare outside autocracies. New rates, any crackdown / deadly force: democracies 28% / 2%, hybrid 40% / 8%, autocracies 55% / 15%. On unseen countries the average miss on deadly force fell from 0.23-0.24 to 0.06-0.07, and on any crackdown from 0.16-0.20 to 0.14-0.15. Each country's V-Dem repression score added nothing on top of the kind of government (rank match 0.36 vs 0.37, 0.71 vs 0.68), so it isn't used.

migration_baseline.text: In the full test, the simulation on its own ranks the countries people really leave at only about 0.03 to 0.06: it barely knows who emigrates.
